parameters.name: Oxygen used per astronaut
parameters.note: NASA's design value for an average crew member. Real use changes with body size and exercise.

parameters.name: Water used per astronaut
parameters.note: A simplified budget for drinking, food and minimal hygiene, based on NASA design figures. Showers and laundry would need more.

parameters.name: Food per astronaut, with packaging
parameters.note: Packaged, ISS-style food.

parameters.name: Water recovered by the recycler
parameters.note: Measured on the ISS: about 93–94% before 2023. In 2023 NASA demonstrated 98% by adding a Brine Processor Assembly. The game keeps 93%.

parameters.name: Water split to make 1 kg of oxygen
parameters.note: Chemistry: 2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂. 36 g of water give 32 g of oxygen.

parameters.name: Cosmic-ray dose on the lunar surface
parameters.note: Dose equivalent measured by China's Chang'e-4 lander in 2019 (1369 µSv per day), near solar minimum. It changes with the Sun's 11-year cycle.

parameters.name: Share of cosmic-ray dose that gets through the habitat walls
parameters.note: A game choice. Thin walls stop little of the very energetic cosmic rays, so most of the dose gets through.

parameters.name: Storm dose inside the habitat, strong storm (NOAA S3)
parameters.note: Scenario estimate. The NOAA S-scale counts fast protons (10 MeV or more) arriving near Earth: S3 means 1,000 per cm² per second per steradian. It does not give the dose inside a habitat, which depends on the storm and on the walls.

parameters.name: Storm dose inside the habitat, severe storm (NOAA S4)
parameters.note: Scenario estimate, like the one above. S4 means 10,000 protons per cm² per second per steradian.

parameters.name: Storm dose blocked by the shelter
parameters.note: Scenario estimate of the order of magnitude: thick regolith or water stops most solar-storm protons, but the exact share depends on the storm and on how thick the shielding is.

parameters.name: Mission dose limit in the game
parameters.note: A game rule: the mission ends if the crew's total dose reaches it. It is inspired by NASA's 30-day limit for blood-forming organs (250 mGy-Eq), which is a different dose quantity. NASA also caps each astronaut's whole-career effective dose at 600 mSv. Real limits guide planning: they are not a line where people suddenly fall ill.

parameters.name: Low-dose goal for the star
parameters.note: A game goal to reward good protection, not a NASA value.

parameters.name: Extra dose for one spacewalk (EVA)
parameters.note: Game estimate, rounded up: outside, the crew loses the little protection of the habitat walls for a few hours.

parameters.name: Battery energy per kilogram
parameters.note: Space-rated lithium-ion packs store about 150–250 Wh per kg. The game battery stores 60 kWh and weighs 250 kg.

parameters.name: Solar array output in full sun
parameters.note: Game value for one array. Real output depends on panel area, Sun tracking and dust.

parameters.name: Habitat power for heat, air and radio
parameters.note: Game value, chosen to make power planning matter.

parameters.name: Oxygen generator output
parameters.note: Game value. Real electrolysers are sized for their crew.

parameters.name: Days before the greenhouse gives food
parameters.note: Game simplification so the effect shows within a mission. Real crops take weeks: lettuce on the ISS takes about a month.

parameters.name: Greenhouse harvest once grown
parameters.note: Game value, with 0.8 kg of oxygen a day from photosynthesis.

parameters.name: Light and shadow periods of each mission
parameters.note: Simplified scenarios, not a real calendar. Near the south pole, sunlight depends on the terrain around each spot: a few high rims are lit most of the time, crater floors almost never. Real calendars are computed from laser maps of the terrain (LOLA).

parameters.name: Crew size
parameters.note: Artemis missions are planned around four astronauts.

oxygen.title: The crew ran out of oxygen
oxygen.what: The oxygen stored in the base reached zero.
oxygen.why: Four astronauts breathe about 3.4 kg of oxygen every day. Oxygen tanks are heavy, and the oxygen generator needs both water and power to make more.
oxygen.principle: Life support is a chain: oxygen depends on water, and making oxygen depends on power. If any link breaks, the whole chain fails.
alternatives: Bring more oxygen tanks, or an oxygen generator for longer missions
Keep the oxygen generator powered — don't let it be the first thing shed
Carry spare parts so a broken generator can be fixed
A greenhouse adds a little oxygen as a backup

water.title: The base ran out of water
water.why: Water is used for drinking, food, hygiene — and to make oxygen and grow plants. Without recycling, every drop used is gone.
water.principle: Closing the loop: recycling 93% of water means you need about 14 times less water from Earth. The longer the mission, the more recycling pays off.
alternatives: Bring a water recycler — on long missions it's lighter than the water it saves
Fix leaks quickly instead of letting them run
Watch the oxygen generator: it turns water into oxygen

food.title: The crew ran out of food
food.what: Food stores stayed empty for several days and mission control ordered an abort.
food.why: Four astronauts eat about 7 kg of packaged food a day. A greenhouse takes a week to produce its first harvest and only covers part of the need.
food.principle: Plan for growth time: biological systems take days or weeks to start producing, so stored food must bridge the gap.
alternatives: Bring enough food crates to cover the days before the first harvest
Keep the greenhouse powered and healthy
Don't count on the greenhouse alone — it's a supplement, not a full supply

power.title: Critical power failure
power.what: The batteries were empty and the solar arrays couldn't power the habitat's core life support for several days.
power.why: When solar generation drops — in shadow, or with dusty panels — the base lives on stored energy. Once batteries run dry, heating, air circulation and CO₂ removal stop.
power.principle: Energy storage must cover critical loads during the longest expected period of low generation, with a safety margin.
alternatives: Bring more battery modules to cover the shadow period
Add solar arrays so batteries recharge faster in sunlight
Switch off non-essential systems (greenhouse first) before the shadow arrives
Clean dusty panels quickly

radiation.title: Radiation dose reached the mission's limit
radiation.what: The crew's radiation dose reached 250 mSv, the limit this game uses for a mission. Mission control brought the crew home early.
radiation.why: The Moon has no magnetic field or thick atmosphere. During a solar storm, the dose inside a thin-walled habitat can rise to tens of mSv per day.
radiation.principle: Radiation protection = time + distance + shielding. You can't control the Sun, so you need mass (regolith, water) between the crew and the storm.
alternatives: Bring a radiation shelter and use it during storms
Keep at least 100 kg of water to build a water wall if you have no shelter
Don't continue normal operations during a severe storm

successLesson.title: Mission accomplished!
successLesson.what: Your crew survived the whole mission and the base kept running.
successLesson.why: You balanced power, water, oxygen, food and radiation protection — even when the storm and the shadow hit.
successLesson.principle: Mission design is about trade-offs: every kilogram and every kilowatt-hour spent on one system is not available for another.
alternatives: Try the mission again with a lighter loadout
Try a different choice during the solar storm and compare the dose
Take on the Commander mission: 28 days at Artemis Base Camp

samples.name: Lunar soil (regolith)
samples.text: Lunar soil grains are sharp and glassy: on the Moon there is no wind or water to round them. They scratch suits and clog seals.

samples.name: Soil from the edge of a shadowed crater
samples.text: Some craters near the south pole never see the Sun. They are cold traps that may hold water ice, one reason Artemis plans to land there.
